findings.summary: The deadline message asserts a cause it has not established: 'the dev server never finished compiling this route'. A 5xx is also treated as not-ready, so a route failing for a genuine product reason would time out under a message blaming compilation. The last status is printed, so a reader can tell, but the sentence over-claims.

One deadline is shared across four sequential probes and computed once. If the first probe consumes most of the 180s the later ones inherit a truncated budget and can report a timeout they would otherwise have survived. Not observed - the whole first test took about 1.1 minutes including all four probes - but latent on a slower machine.

The case named 'leaves the rest of the config byte-identical to the file under review' no longer compares bytes; it compares LF-normalised text. The change is correct - a byte comparison was testing the checkout's line endings rather than the rendering - but the name now overstates what it asserts.

Splitting the POSIX half into its own case re-runs the entrypoint script, so the mode assertion inspects a different temporary run than the content assertion. Equivalent in practice - same script, same environment - but it is duplicated work and a reader may assume both assertions describe one run.

ensurePermission is declared at line 97, above the ALL_ACTIONS and MODULES constants at 109-110 whose types it references. Type-only references are hoisted so tsc is satisfied, but the file reads backwards at that point.

ST-002 bounds a tool body as a fraction of total file length (source.length/4 and /2). That catches the actual regression, which over-read by roughly fourteen times, but the thresholds are heuristic and drift as the file grows. The semantic bound - modelsRead('searchLeads') equals exactly ['lead'] - is the assertion doing the real work.

Checked and clear: the four probe routes declare no rateLimit spec, and an unauthenticated request has no ctx, so the handler's rate-limit branch is skipped entirely. The probe consumes no login or per-user budget on any run.

Checked and clear: apiReady memoises the promise, so a rejection is cached and every later caller fails the same way. For a readiness gate that is the correct behaviour - if the API never became ready, failing fast is right - and the promise is returned and awaited immediately, so no unhandled rejection is possible.

The rewrite converted this file's line endings from CRLF to LF in the working tree. core.autocrlf=true normalises to LF in the index, so the committed content is identical either way and there is no functional consequence; but it is an undeclared side effect, and it is why this file now passes npm run format:check while most of the repository does not.

notes: Scope: the final SPEC-0004 diff - 10 files across TESTS, SCRIPTS, PLAYWRIGHT/HARNESS, DOCUMENTATION, plus the governance artefacts.
